## Smith Douglas Homes: Built on Consistency


**November 13, 2026**


[back to posts](https://www.bc.com/blog/)


In production homebuilding, everything is connected.


A pricing decision can impact the availability and reliability of your trades. A materials issue can affect the schedule and margins.


And, of course, a delay in almost any step can ripple through the entire build. That’s why[Smith Douglas Homes](https://www.smithdouglas.com/) sees operational excellence as key to their success.


Courtesy of Smith Douglas Homes


That’s where Bentley Reece, one of the company’s Trade Relations Managers, comes in.


“The biggest challenge is the inconsistencies in the market,” Reece said. “My job is to make sure we have the right trades and the right vendors and the right products in place for our construction teams to keep moving.”


Reece brings a unique perspective to the process.


A third-generation funeral director and embalmer, he entered homebuilding after spending about a decade in the funeral business. He returned to college, earned a degree in construction management from Kennesaw State University, and joined Smith Douglas Homes as a construction manager trainee.


Today, his responsibilities reflect how many factors go into making a successful home builder. Not only does he manage relationships with trades and other vendors from the earliest stages of a new community to the final walkthrough, he is also responsible for construction operations, cost evaluations, improving production efficiency, and helping construction teams resolve issues across the division.


“We have to keep all the moving pieces aligned,” he said, explaining that as a production homebuilder that just surpassed 20,000 completed builds, Smith Douglas Homes must maintain discipline to keep customers happy and margins relatively strong in a business where margins are always tight.


“I used to ask, how can I fix things one house at a time?” he said. “Now, I’m asking myself, my team, and my vendors, how do I not have this issue on the next 50 homes?”


### **People + Process = Prosperity**


Smith Douglas Homes was founded in 2008 by homebuilding veteran Tom Bradbury in Atlanta, Georgia, following the global financial crisis. As the company grew, the company established a highly disciplined, schedule-driven building model — the Rteam Production Model — designed to build affordable, high-quality homes. Over the next decade, it expanded across the Southeastern United States and into Texas. In January 2024, the company reached a major milestone by going public on the New York Stock Exchange. In many ways, the Rteam model is


Courtesy of Smith Douglas Homes


Smith Douglas’ not-so-secret sauce. It’s something they see as a value-add to their trade partners and customers, as well as the municipalities where they build. The Rteam model is based on four core principles, including:


- Relationships: building strong, collaborative connections with vendors and subcontractors;


- Real-time: proactively sharing up-to-date information, including schedules and job status;


- Readiness and Responsibility: ensuring everyone is ready and accountable for their role in the build; and


- Repeatable and Responsible Growth: keeping work predictable and steady without a lot of stop and go.


The Rteam model is more than a philosophy. It is how they work. All Smith Douglas communities are organized around, and assigned to, geographically defined Rteams, typically covering no more than a 20-mile radius.


Each team works with a consistent group of trades and vendors, creating familiarity with the home plans, expectations, and schedules. It keeps everyone involved in the build working together efficiently and effectively, allowing them to deliver on their company mission of providing “a home that is priced below the competition, but feels like a home that is worth far more.”


### **Consistency Starts with the Right Products**


According to Reece, consistency is at the heart of the Rteam approach. It’s crucial for a number of reasons, including the company’s compressed build schedules, which can be as tight as 45 days.


“The schedule is the lifeblood of Smith Douglas Homes,” Reece said. “We need products and partners that can perform repeatedly across all of our divisions,”


This means the team relies on vendors who can keep up with Smith Douglas’ need for speed — without sacrificing quality — across multiple markets and home styles. It’s why Reece chooses Boise Cascade Engineered Wood Products. “We don’t really ever have problems with BCIs,” he said. “Our construction managers aren’t having to solve any unnecessary problems in the field, and our framers can put up a house within five days when there are no problems with the materials.”


For a production builder, that consistency extends beyond the material itself.[BCI](https://www.bc.com/ewp/bci-joists/)


®


joists are a stocked item, which means lead time can be a fraction compared to other floor systems. A framing package that is delivered on time and performs as expected helps ensure no unnecessary delays in other parts of the schedule as well.


“It’s just an all-around great fit to keep everything going smoothly.” Of course, in a business as competitive as production homebuilding, consistent quality isn’t the only factor builders must consider. The numbers have to pencil out, and for Smith Douglas, they do.


“We build homes with very tight margins,” says Reece. “So, I’m always looking at a hard cost, but I don’t believe the cheapest number on a bid automatically is always the lowest cost.”


If a product creates additional labor, delays the schedule, or requires someone to return to the jobsite to fix a problem, the initial savings can quickly disappear.


“I’m really looking for the best overall value when I’m building a home,” he said. “And that’s what I’ve been given and what I’ve seen with Boise Cascade in 14+ years in new home construction.”


### **A Floor System Built for Repeatability**


Courtesy of Smith Douglas Homes


Evaluating not simply the surface-level costs of a product or vendor, but considering the total value they bring, is central to both the Rteam philosophy and a big contributor to successfully building at scale, according to Reece. This mindset recently led Smith Douglas to expand its use of BCI Joists, transitioning from open-web floor trusses across builds in Chattanooga and around Atlanta.


The decision wasn’t simply about trying something “new,” it was about finding a floor system that could support a consistent, repeatable building process. “With us being a production homebuilder trying to hit a 45-day schedule, BCI joists have really helped streamline that across the board,” he said. “With that engineered system we can keep a constantly repeated home on schedule… that process really matters.”


While it can take some time to educate trades on a new product, the benefits of Boise Cascade BCI joists are proving to outweigh the early part of the journey. Now, the result is consistency in the installation process and minimal floor squeaks in the finished home.


### **Relationships with a Capital R**


There’s no doubt about it: Smith Douglas Homes is a tremendously successful production homebuilder, ranking #33 in


*Builder Magazine* ’s annual Builder 100 list and with sales closing in on a billion dollars annually. But when Bentley Reece describes what makes the company unique, the first thing is not the buttoned-up processes and operational excellence, it’s the strength of the relationships.


Before joining the company, he assumed that materials, schedules, and numbers were what mattered most to a production builder. “They obviously do,” he said. “But I’ve learned that we don’t just look at people as another number.”


It makes sense. Because for a production builder, operational efficiency isn’t created by any single decision. It’s built by putting the right people, products, and processes together — and then making them work together, consistently, again and again. “Our team is what really separates us from the other big guys,” he reflects. “We have a lot of people who treat us as family, and we treat them as family as well.”
